chunks: I wrote to Abu Muhammad (peace be upon him) asking him: How does a servant worship his Lord when he cannot see Him?
So he (peace be upon him) signed: O Abu Yusuf! My Chief, my Master, and the Bestower of blessings upon me and upon my forefathers is too Majestic to be seen.
He said: And I asked him whether the Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) had seen his Lord.
So he (peace be upon him) signed: Indeed God, the Blessed and Exalted, caused His Messenger to see, through his heart, from the light of His Magnificence, what He willed.

key_terms.بِقَلْبِهِ: Through his heart — spiritual/interior perception as opposed to physical ocular vision
key_terms.جَلَّ: Is too Majestic/Exalted — expresses the transcendence and incomparability of God
key_terms.نُورِ عَظَمَتِهِ: The light of His Magnificence — divine self-disclosure through light, not physical form
key_terms.وَقَّعَ: Signed (a written response/rescript) — a technical term for a written response from an Imam to a petitioner's written question
key_terms.يُرَى: To be seen/perceived — the key theological question of ru'yat Allah (vision of God)

ai.seo_question: Did the Prophet Muhammad see God, and can God be seen in Islam according to Imam al-Askari?
ai.summary: This hadith records a written exchange between a companion (Yaqoub ibn Is'haq) and Imam Hasan al-Askari (AS), in which two fundamental theological questions about the vision of God are addressed. The Imam affirms that God is too transcendent (jall) to be perceived by physical sight, and clarifies that the Prophet Muhammad's 'vision' of his Lord was a spiritual illumination received through the heart — not a physical sighting. This teaching is central to the Shia theological position against the Ash'ari view that God can be seen in the hereafter.
